short: Seven kingdoms fought for two and a half centuries until Qin swallowed the rest.
full:
By 475 BCE seven states dominated the Zhou world: Qin, Chu, Qi, Yan, Han, Zhao and Wei. Each dropped the pretence of vassalage and took the royal title, and each fought the others with armies numbering in the hundreds of thousands rather than the aristocratic chariot forces of earlier centuries. The crossbow, mass-produced in bronze with interchangeable trigger mechanisms, made a conscripted farmer lethal to a nobleman. Cavalry, walled frontier lines and long sieges followed. Sunzi's Art of War belongs to this world.

States that survived did so by reorganising themselves. The reforms Shang Yang carried out in Qin from 356 BCE abolished hereditary privilege, tied rank to battlefield merit, registered households and taxed them directly — the Legalist model of a state as an instrument for war and agriculture. It worked. Between 230 and 221 BCE Qin armies destroyed the other six kingdoms in turn. The same years produced the Hundred Schools of Thought: Confucian, Daoist, Mohist and Legalist arguments about how people should be governed, conducted while the killing went on.
